title: What Bill Watterson Teaches Teachers
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart uses The Complete Calvin and Hobbes — a favorite gift for his own kids — as an extended metaphor for teaching. Building on his earlier "cosmos" framing (a classroom as an alternate, ordered world students are invited into), he argues that students themselves are a cosmos: the mischief-making Calvin a teacher sees in class is only a sliver of a much fuller imaginative person. He draws several career lessons from Bill Watterson's own choices — refusing merchandising and a TV adaptation to protect the strip's integrity, and retiring the strip at the height of its popularity rather than running it into decline. Pairing Watterson's retirement letter with a line from Jim Burke's own retirement interview ("It's always better to leave when you're not sure that you should than to stay around until everyone's sure that you should"), Stuart frames knowing when to say no and when to quit as forms of the same underlying discipline: protecting finite time and energy for the work that matters most.
points: Stuart extends his "classroom as cosmos" metaphor to students themselves — arguing that what a teacher sees of a "mischievous" kid in class is only a sliver of the fuller cosmos of that student's inner life and interests.
Watterson's refusal of merchandising and a TV adaptation is used as a model of professional discipline: protecting the integrity of core work by saying no to profitable but compromising expansions.

Pairing Watterson's and Jim Burke's near-identical reasoning for retiring ("leave while you still love it," at the height rather than the decline) frames knowing when to quit as a skill, not a failure.

The essay argues teachers, like Watterson, should bring genuine craftsmanship and their own idiosyncratic interests into curricular constraints rather than settling for the dullness schools can default to.
quotes: Your classroom is an alternate world from the one your students normally inhabit. Or at least, it should be. It's a cosmos—Latinized from the Greek kosmos: a good order, an orderly arrangement; a world.
But when you read Calvin and Hobbes, a related truth emerges: our kids are a cosmos, too.
It turns out Calvin's a lot more than a first grade mischief-maker. He's a cosmos. What his teacher sees is only a sliver of who he is.
In rereading Watterson's strip, I find in myself a growing capacity for relishing a bit of the mischief some of my students bring to class, too.
Watterson was not just insightful — he was an artist, and he lavished his excellence at a level uncalled for by his medium.

Watterson was something rare in today's world: a human being in touch with their finitude. He had only so much time, so much energy. He wanted to keep these precious resources focused on where he could do his greatest good — on his comic strip.

It's always better to leave when you're not sure that you should than to stay around until everyone's sure that you should." In the interview Burke expanded on this, saying, "I wanted to leave while I still loved it.

My interests have shifted however, and I believe I've done what I can do within the constraints of daily deadlines and small panels. I am eager to work at a more thoughtful pace, with fewer artistic compromises.
